subsystems.name: Chassis organism
subsystems.role: the host cell whose genome is stripped down and rebuilt so its behaviour is predictable.

subsystems.name: Designed genome
subsystems.role: a DNA sequence written on a computer specifying every gene the organism needs, plus added functions.

subsystems.name: DNA synthesis and assembly
subsystems.role: turns the digital design into physical DNA and joins the pieces.

subsystems.name: Genome installation
subsystems.role: transplants the finished genome into a recipient cell so it 'boots' and starts running the new program.

subsystems.name: Function module
subsystems.role: the reason the organism exists — making a drug, sensing a pollutant, or breaking a chemical down.

subsystems.name: Biocontainment
subsystems.role: keeps the organism from surviving or spreading where it should not.

buildSteps.title: Pick the job and the chassis
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether the organism must make a molecule, degrade one, or sense a condition, then choose a host and estimate the metabolic burden.

buildSteps.title: Design the genome in software
buildSteps.detail: Genes, promoters and control elements are specified computationally, with models predicting which designs will actually work in a cell.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the DNA
buildSteps.detail: Short strands are made chemically and joined into larger fragments, with sequencing used to reject errors before they propagate.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and debug the genome
buildSteps.detail: Fragments are stitched together inside yeast or bacteria, and faulty regions are located by growth tests and sequencing.

buildSteps.title: Install and boot the cell
buildSteps.detail: The assembled genome is transplanted into a recipient cell, which is then screened for the intended behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Engineer containment
buildSteps.detail: Kill switches and nutrient dependencies are added, and escape and mutation rates are measured under realistic conditions.

buildSteps.title: Test in a controlled environment
buildSteps.detail: Performance, stability and safety are checked in sealed bioreactors or contained mesocosms before any outdoor trial.

buildSteps.title: Scale production or release
buildSteps.detail: For medicine the organism is grown in a fermenter under pharmaceutical rules; for bioremediation, staged field trials with monitoring come first.

prerequisites.why: writing whole genomes is still slow and error-prone at megabase scale.
no model reliably predicts how an engineered genome behaves inside a living cell.
CRISPR-based editing and base editing make many small changes practical.
kill switches have been demonstrated in the lab but not proven over years in the environment.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory and monitoring framework for released organisms
prerequisites.why: without agreed rules and detection methods, environmental deployment cannot be approved at scale.

pathway.milestone: a bacterial cell with a chemically synthesised genome was made in 2010, and a reduced minimal genome followed in 2016
pathway.unlocks: proof that a designed genome can run a living cell.

pathway.milestone: the international synthetic yeast project is building all of a yeast's chromosomes from scratch
pathway.unlocks: methods for large, heavily edited genomes in a well-understood organism.

pathway.milestone: engineered microbes in contained fermenters producing medicines, enzymes and materials
pathway.unlocks: commercial experience with designed organisms, without release into nature.

pathway.milestone: contained field trials of engineered organisms for pollutant breakdown
pathway.unlocks: evidence on survival, spread and actual cleanup performance.

pathway.milestone: licensed therapeutic and bioremediation organisms in routine use
pathway.unlocks: treatments and waste cleanup that work where chemistry is too expensive or too blunt.
